mainTopic: The dowry and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's rule; the husband's duties to his wife as exchanges for his rights; and whether her food is a Torah obligation.
overview: The גמרא first suggests that an argument about the dowry (did the husband acquire it or not) matches an older argument between רבי אלעזר בן עזריה and the רבנן about the extra amount in the כתובה. It then rejects that link. Everyone can follow רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, because the husband's extra is given only on condition of the wedding, while the dowry from her side is given for the families joining, which already happened at אירוסין. Next the גמרא opens a new section on the משנה's line about feeding the wife. A ברייתא teaches that the חכמים paired each of the husband's duties with a right he receives. The גמרא fills in a missing line: food for her earnings, ransom for the produce of her property, and burial for her כתובה. It explains that 'therefore he eats the produce' means he really eats it and must ransom her from his own money. אביי explains the pairings: everyday duties go with everyday rights, and rare ones with rare ones. Finally, רבא says one תנא holds that food is a Torah obligation, and a ברייתא shows that both opinions find food in שמות 21:10, arguing only about which word teaches it.

steps.title: Linking the dowry argument to an older argument
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's reason (the husband wrote the extra only on condition of marrying her). It then suggests that whoever says the husband did not acquire the dowry follows רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, and whoever says he did acquire it follows the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Because he wrote it for her only on condition that he would marry her.' So the one who says the husband did not acquire holds like רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, and the one who says he did acquire holds like the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רבי אלעזר בן עזריה and suggests that the current argument about the dowry is really the same as his argument with the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says a commitment in the כתובה made before the wedding depends on the wedding actually happening. If that idea also applies to the dowry, then the opinion that the husband 'did not acquire' fits him, and the opinion that he 'did acquire' fits the רבנן. This is only a suggestion, and the next step will challenge it.

keyTerms.meaning: He acquired (gained the right to the money)
On condition that he actually marries her (brings her into his home)
The majority of the Sages, who disagree with him

steps.confusionAlert: The first line is not a new statement. It is the end of a quote of רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's reason, which started before this point.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא כָּתַב לָהּ אֶלָּא עַל מְנָת לְכוֹנְסָהּ.
phrases.english: for he wrote it for her only on condition that he would marry her.

steps.triggerLanguage: למאן דאמר לא זכה כרבי אלעזר בן עזריה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the quote of the תנאים begun before this point and applies it to the argument about the dowry.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The suggestion: 'did not acquire' follows רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, and 'did acquire' follows the רבנן.

steps.title: No, everyone can follow רבי אלעזר בן עזריה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Both opinions can agree with רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, because he only spoke about money going from the husband to the wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone holds like רבי אלעזר בן עזריה. The one who says 'did not acquire' holds like him. And the one who says 'did acquire' will say: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה only said his rule about money going from him to her, because he wrote it for her only on condition of marrying her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and says the argument about the dowry does not have to depend on the older argument at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is that רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's rule has limits. It covers only what the husband gives the wife, the extra in the כתובה, since he clearly meant it as a wedding commitment. So even the opinion that the husband 'did acquire' the dowry can agree with him.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
He only said his ruling up to this point (in this case)
From his to hers: what the husband gives the wife

phrases.english: No, everyone agrees
with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
The one who says he did not acquire —
holds like Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya,
and the one who says he did acquire —

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya only said his ruling
about what goes from him to her,
phrases.notes: He means the extra amount the husband adds to her כתובה.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא כָּתַב לָהּ אֶלָּא עַל מְנָת לְכוֹנְסָהּ.
phrases.english: for he wrote it for her only on condition that he would marry her.

steps.triggerLanguage: לא, דכולי עלמא כרבי אלעזר בן עזריה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 1's link between the two arguments.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the claim that the 'did acquire' opinion must disagree with רבי אלעזר בן עזריה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 1 assumed רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's rule covers all money tied to the marriage. In fact it covers only what the husband gives the wife.

steps.title: Why the dowry is different: it is given for the family bond
steps.stepSummary: Money going from the wife's side to the husband is a different case. Even רבי אלעזר בן עזריה agrees the husband acquires it, because it is given for the families becoming connected, and that connection already happened at אירוסין.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for what goes from her to him, even רבי אלעזר בן עזריה agrees, because it is given for the sake of becoming related by marriage, and they have already become related.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its rejection by explaining why the dowry does not depend on the wedding actually taking place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each kind of money is tied to its own reason. The husband's extra is tied to bringing her into his home, which never happened. The father's dowry is tied to the families becoming connected, and that already happened at אירוסין. So the husband can acquire the dowry even according to רבי אלעזר בן עזריה.

keyTerms.meaning: From hers to his: what comes from the wife's side to the husband
Agrees
Becoming related by marriage (the families joining)

steps.whatToRemember: The direction of the money matters. Husband to wife (the תוספת) depends on the full marriage. The wife's side to the husband (the dowry) depends only on the families being joined, which already happened at אירוסין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common method in the גמרא: a disagreement between אמוראים does not have to match a disagreement between תנאים, if one side can limit the תנא's rule to a narrower case.

phrases.english: But regarding what goes from her to him,
phrases.notes: This is the dowry her father gave.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה מוֹדֵי,
phrases.english: even Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya agrees,
since it is given because of becoming related by marriage,
and they have already become related.

steps.triggerLanguage: אבל מדידה לדידיה אפילו רבי אלעזר בן עזריה מודי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the rejection from step 2 by explaining the other direction of money.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between the two cases (which direction the money goes and why it was given)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה's rule would cancel any money tied to a marriage that never fully happened.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dowry is given for the family bond, which already exists, so even רבי אלעזר בן עזריה agrees the husband acquires it.

steps.title: New section: the husband's duties are exchanges for his rights
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה's line about the husband's duty to feed his wife. It brings a ברייתא: the חכמים set up her food in exchange for her earnings, and her burial in exchange for her כתובה. Therefore the husband eats the produce of her property.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He is obligated in her food, etc.' The רבנן taught: They instituted her food in exchange for her handiwork, and her burial in exchange for her כתובה. Therefore the husband eats the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes the משנה's words and brings a ברייתא that explains the husband's duties as fair exchanges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא pairs each duty with a right. He feeds her and receives her earnings. He buries her and inherits what is written in her כתובה. The ending, 'therefore the husband eats the produce,' is stated as following from these pairs, so pay attention to how it connects.

keyTerms.meaning: They (the חכמים) instituted
Food and support
Her handiwork: the money she earns from her work
Burial
Produce: the income from her property

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea of 'this in exchange for that' becomes the basic framework for the money relationship between husband and wife in the rest of the discussion.

phrases.english: He is obligated in her food, etc.
The Rabbis taught:
They instituted her food
in exchange for her handiwork,
and her burial in exchange for her ketubah,
phrases.notes: He means the husband inherits what she brought into the marriage, which is written in her כתובה.

phrases.english: therefore, the husband eats the produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: חייב במזונותיה וכו׳ תנו רבנן תיקנו מזונותיה תחת מעשה ידיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the dowry discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food is in exchange for her handiwork, and burial is in exchange for her כתובה. Therefore the husband eats the produce of her property.

steps.title: Produce was never mentioned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised that the ברייתא concludes 'therefore the husband eats the produce,' when nothing about produce came before.
steps.simpleTranslation: Produce? Who mentioned them at all?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a problem in the ברייתא from Step 4. Its ending talks about פֵּירוֹת, but nothing earlier in it talked about פֵּירוֹת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said food is in exchange for her earnings and burial is in exchange for her כתובה. The word 'therefore' should follow from something already said, but neither of those items has anything to do with produce. So the ending seems to come out of nowhere.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce, the income that comes from the wife's property
Who mentioned them? Used when a source talks about something it never brought up
Mentioned

phrases.english: Produce, who mentioned them?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא quoted in Step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The closing line of the ברייתא: 'therefore the husband eats the produce'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A conclusion introduced by 'therefore' must follow from something already stated, but produce was never stated.

steps.title: Words are missing: ransom in exchange for produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is missing a line: the husband must ransom his wife in exchange for eating the produce of her property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Words are missing, and this is what it teaches: They set up her food in exchange for her earnings, her ransom in exchange for the produce, and her burial in exchange for her כתובה. Therefore the husband eats the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by adding a missing middle line to the ברייתא. Once that line is added, the mention of פֵּירוֹת makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The added line is that the husband must pay for her פִּדְיוֹן (ransom from captivity) in exchange for eating her produce. Now there are three pairs instead of two, and the ending about produce follows from the middle pair.

keyTerms.meaning: Words are missing from the text
And this is what it is teaching
Her ransom, paying to free her if she is captured
Her earnings, the work of her hands
Her burial

steps.whatToRemember: There are three pairs: food for earnings, ransom for produce, burial for the כתובה.

phrases.english: It is missing words, and this is what it teaches:
They set up her food in exchange for her earnings,
and her ransom in exchange for the produce,
and her burial in exchange for her כתובה.
Therefore the husband eats the produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 5 by filling in missing words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא had only two pairs, so the mention of produce had no source
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא really has three pairs, and the ransom-for-produce pair explains the ending

steps.title: What does the word 'therefore' add?
steps.stepSummary: Even with the missing line added, the גמרא asks what the word 'therefore' is coming to teach.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the word לְפִיכָךְ adds. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ransom is paid in exchange for produce, it is obvious that the husband gets the produce. So the word 'therefore' seems extra, and the גמרא wants to know what new point it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore, consequently
What
What is 'therefore' adding?

phrases.english: What is 'therefore'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word in the corrected ברייתא from Step 6
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new teaching the word 'therefore' brings

steps.title: He eats the produce now and pays ransom from his own money
steps.stepSummary: 'Therefore' teaches that the husband actually eats the produce instead of saving it for a ransom, because then he must pay her ransom from his own money no matter what.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: he should not eat the produce but save it, because if he eats it, he will hold back and not ransom her. So it teaches us that this way is better: sometimes the produce does not add up to enough, and this way he ransoms her from his own money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that 'therefore' tells us the husband really eats the produce. It is better for the wife this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think he should save the produce, since a husband who has used it up might not want to pay a ransom. But if the ransom came only from saved produce, there might not be enough. Since he eats the produce, he must pay the full ransom from his own pocket.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said, introducing a mistaken idea
He should leave them aside, save them
It teaches us
Better, preferable
From his own money

steps.whatToRemember: The husband eats the produce, and he must ransom his wife from his own money even if the produce would not have been enough.

phrases.english: You might have said:
he should not eat them,
he should leave them aside.
For if so, he will hold back and not ransom her,
phrases.notes: 'If so' means if he eats the produce. Then he might not want to pay the ransom himself.

phrases.english: It teaches us that this is better.
Sometimes they do not add up,
phrases.notes: Literally 'do not fill up.' The saved produce might not cover the whole ransom.

phrases.english: and he ransoms her from his own money.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Therefore' teaches that he really eats the produce, which is better for her because he must then pay the full ransom from his own money

steps.title: Why not switch the pairs around?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the pairings themselves: maybe her food should be paired with the produce instead.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about the rule itself, not the wording. Why pair each duty with these specific rights and not the other way around? This sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing in the ברייתא explains why food goes with earnings and ransom goes with produce. The challenger says the pairs could be switched, for example food in exchange for produce. The גמרא will need to justify the order it gave.

keyTerms.meaning: I can reverse it, a challenge saying the pairing could be switched
Reverse, switch around
I

phrases.english: But I can reverse it!
phrases.notes: He means: why not pair her food with the produce, and her ransom with her earnings?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of the ברייתא to questioning its pairings
steps.kashyaTarget: The pairings in the ברייתא: food for earnings, ransom for produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No reason has been given for these specific pairs, so they could just as well be reversed.

steps.title: Everyday duty paired with everyday right
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the חכמים paired the husband's everyday duty, feeding her, with his everyday right, her earnings. The less common duties were paired with the less common rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The חכמים matched something that happens all the time with something that happens all the time, and something uncommon with something uncommon.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge from step 9, which asked why her food was not paired with the produce instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food is needed every single day, and a wife's earnings (מעשה ידיה) also come in every day, so those two belong together. Ransom (פדיון) is rarely needed and does not happen often, so it was paired with produce (פירות), the other arrangement in the pairings. Matching by how often each thing comes up explains the system.

keyTerms.meaning: They (the חכמים) instituted
Common, something that comes up regularly
Uncommon, something that comes up rarely

steps.whatToRemember: The rabbinic pairings follow a simple rule: everyday for everyday (food for earnings), rare for rare.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
They instituted a common thing in exchange for a common thing,
phrases.notes: Food is needed every day, and her earnings come in every day. That is the common pair.

phrases.english: and an uncommon thing in exchange for an uncommon thing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 9 about why the pairings were set up this way.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the reasoning behind the pairings: they are matched by how often each item comes up.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Food could just as well have been paired with produce.
steps.terutzMaskana: Food is paired with earnings because both are everyday matters. Rare matters are paired with rare matters.

steps.title: רבא: this תנא holds food is a Torah obligation
steps.stepSummary: רבא states that the תנא of the ברייתא he is about to quote holds that a husband's duty to feed his wife is מדאורייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This תנא holds that food is required by the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא makes a new claim about a wife's food, and he is setting up a ברייתא that will prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion treated food as part of the rabbinic package of pairings. רבא raises a new point: according to this תנא, the obligation to feed her is not only rabbinic but comes from the Torah itself.

keyTerms.meaning: A sage of the משנה period whose teaching is quoted
Food, the wife's sustenance
From the Torah, Torah law

phrases.english: Rava said:
This tanna holds
that food is from the Torah,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הַאי תַּנָּא סָבַר מְזוֹנוֹת מִדְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about where the food obligation comes from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to this תנא, a husband's duty to feed his wife is a Torah obligation.

steps.title: The ברייתא reads שארה as food
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא reads the three words of שמות 21:10. שארה means food (proved from מיכה), כסותה means clothing, and עונתה means marital intimacy (proved from בראשית).
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: 'Her שאר' means food, as the verse says, 'who ate the שאר of my people.' 'Her clothing' means just what it says. 'Her עונה' means the marital intimacy the Torah speaks of, as the verse says, 'if you afflict (תענה) my daughters.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings the ברייתא that proves his claim. It explains each of the three things a husband may not hold back from his wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word שאר is shown to mean food, because in מיכה people 'eat' שאר. So the Torah's own words require food, which is רבא's point. The word עונה is tied to 'affliction' in בראשית, where holding back marital intimacy is called afflicting a wife.

keyTerms.meaning: Her שאר, the first of the three things in the verse
Her clothing
Her עונה, the third thing in the verse
According to its plain meaning
And so it says, introducing a supporting verse

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
"Her she'er": this is food,
phrases.notes: The ברייתא is reading שמות 21:10, the three things a husband may not hold back.

phrases.english: and so it says:
"Who ate the flesh (she'er) of my people."
"Her clothing": as it sounds.
"Her onah": this is the marital intimacy spoken of in the Torah,
and so it says:
"If you afflict my daughters."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for רבא's claim in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's claim that food is a Torah obligation
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא reading שארה in שמות 21:10 as food, supported by מיכה 3:3.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר reverses the readings
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads שארה as marital intimacy (proved from ויקרא) and עונתה as food (proved from דברים). כסותה still means clothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: 'Her שאר' means marital intimacy, as the verse says, 'No man shall come near any of his own שאר to uncover nakedness.' 'Her clothing' means just what it says. 'Her עונה' means food, as the verse says, 'He afflicted you (ויענך) and made you hungry.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with רבי אלעזר, who swaps the meanings of the first and third words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי אלעזר, שאר is a word used for close relatives in the context of forbidden relations, so it means intimacy. עינוי is linked to hunger in דברים, so עונה means food. Even with the swap, food is still written in the verse, so the Torah obligation of מזונות stands either way.

keyTerms.meaning: His close relative, literally 'the flesh of his flesh'
And He afflicted you

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי אלעזר denies that food is from the Torah. He only moves food from the word שארה to the word עונתה.
steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions in the ברייתא find food in the verse. They only argue about which word teaches it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says:
"Her she'er": this is marital intimacy.
And so it says:
"No man shall, to any of his close kin (she'er),
come near to uncover nakedness."
"Her clothing": as it sounds.
"Her onah": this is food,
and so it says:
"And He afflicted you and made you hungry."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: שְׁאֵרָהּ זוֹ עוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second opinion in the same ברייתא, swapping the meanings of the first and third words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שארה means marital intimacy and עונתה means food. Food is still a Torah obligation.
